evidenceAudit.scope: Bleeding from the genital tract from 24 weeks of pregnancy to birth in India: severity, placenta praevia and abruption, assessment without digital examination, resuscitation and blood products, anti-D, corticosteroids, delivery decisions and third-stage management, using RCOG Green-top Guideline 63 and WHO antenatal corticosteroid recommendations (2022), because no Indian APH guideline with these details could be opened.
findings: Definitions (spotting, minor under 50 mL, major 50–1000 mL without shock, massive over 1000 mL or shock), no digital examination until praevia excluded, investigations by severity with 4 units cross-matched for major or massive bleeding, Kleihauer and anti-D at least 500 IU after 20 weeks, corticosteroids 24+0–34+6 weeks, no tocolysis in abruption or major APH, immediate delivery for maternal or fetal compromise, resuscitation and blood product targets, and active third-stage management checked against RCOG GTG 63.
Dexamethasone 6 mg IM 12-hourly for 4 doses (or betamethasone 12 mg IM 24-hourly for 2) between 24 and 34 weeks checked against WHO 2022 recommendation 1.9.
unverifiedSections: No Indian national APH guideline was opened; the Indian PPH topic and Safe Birth practice should be used alongside.
RCOG and WHO corticosteroid gestational windows differ slightly (34+6 vs 34 weeks); both are shown.
Magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection is not covered by the opened sources.
Drug cautions, contraindications and renal or hepatic adjustment lines without a source tag are general pharmacology statements and need formulary confirmation.

pathophysiology.summary: Antepartum haemorrhage complicates 3–5% of pregnancies and is a leading cause of maternal and perinatal death (RCOG GTG 63). The important causes are placenta praevia (placenta in the lower segment, typically painless bright bleeding) and placental abruption (premature separation, typically painful with a tense uterus, and bleeding may be concealed). Severity is judged by blood loss and signs of shock, but visible loss underestimates abruption. Digital vaginal examination is avoided until praevia is excluded by ultrasound. Care focuses on resuscitation, assessing mother and fetus, steroids if preterm, anti-D if RhD-negative, and timely delivery.
keyMechanisms: Placenta praevia: lower-segment stretching shears the placenta from the decidua, causing painless bleeding.
Abruption: haemorrhage into the decidua separates the placenta, often with pain and uterine irritability.
Large abruption can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation and fetal hypoxia.
Hypovolaemia threatens maternal organs and placental perfusion.

symptoms: Abdominal pain, back pain, tense uterus (abruption)
physicalSigns: Tachycardia, hypotension in major or massive bleeding
redFlags: Blood loss over 1000 mL or shock: massive APH (RCOG)
Maternal or fetal compromise: deliver immediately (RCOG 13.1)
Fetal death with abruption: coagulopathy risk
Known placenta praevia with any bleeding

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate
actions: ABCD; oxygen 10–15 L/min; two 14G cannulae (RCOG Appendix).
Warmed crystalloid up to 2 L and/or colloid 1–2 L until blood available (RCOG).
Cross-matched blood; group-specific or O RhD-negative if urgent (RCOG).

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: No digital vaginal examination until praevia excluded (RCOG).

clinicalManagement.title: Blood products
actions: FFP 4 units per 6 units of red cells or if PT/APTT over 1.5 times control; platelets if below 50 x10^9/L; cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen below 1 g/L (RCOG).
Targets: Hb above 8 g/dL, platelets above 75 x10^9/L, fibrinogen above 1 g/L (RCOG).

clinicalManagement.title: Delivery decision
actions: Maternal or fetal compromise: deliver now, usually by caesarean unless in established labour (RCOG 13.1).
Bleeding settled, no compromise, before 37 weeks: no evidence for elective preterm delivery (RCOG).
No tocolysis in major APH, instability or abruption (RCOG 11).

clinicalManagement.title: Steroids, anti-D, third stage
actions: Corticosteroids if 24–34 weeks and birth likely (WHO 2022; RCOG).
Active management of the third stage; anticipate PPH (RCOG 13.4).
